sentences.text: Coloborhynchus is a genus of pterodactyloid pterosaur, a type of flying reptile, classified within the family Anhangueridae.
However, some scientific studies have recovered this animal as a member of the family Ornithocheiridae instead.

The genus name Coloborhynchus means "maimed beak," referring to the damaged and eroded condition of the original fossil, while the specific name clavirostris means "key snout," referring to the shape of the snout in cross-section.
According to a 2008 re-evaluation, Coloborhynchus clavirostris can only be differentiated from relatives based on a unique combination of tooth socket positions.
The final two preserved pairs of teeth in Coloborhynchus pointed downward, a feature that helps distinguish it from other species.

The rosette at the tip of the Coloborhynchus snout was robust and box-shaped, unlike the rounded and spoon-shaped rosettes of related Anhanguera species, and the front margin of the snout was straight and began at the tip, unlike the curved margins that start further back in related species.
Coloborhynchus was once considered the largest known toothed pterosaur, but this record is now held by the closely related genus Tropeognathus.

The possible species Coloborhynchus capito is considered the largest known toothed pterosaur and the second largest known ornithocheirid, and if proportions held, a specimen could have had a skull length of up to 75 cm and an estimated wingspan of 7 meters.
The genus Coloborhynchus was named by Richard Owen in 1874, and the species Coloborhynchus clavirostris, named by Owen in 1874, is the type species of the genus.
Owen named the species based on a partial snout fossil found in the Hastings beds of the Wealden Group in East Sussex, England.
Richard Owen originally defined the genus by the high position of the front tooth pairs on the side of the upper jaws, considering this the defining characteristic of the genus.
The genus was revived in 1994 when Yuong-Nam Lee named C. wadleighi based on a snout found in 1992 in the Paw Paw Formation of Texas.

A second specimen of Coloborhynchus showing unique features was reported to Alexander Kellner by Darren Naish in 2007, likely representing a second specimen of C. clavirostris that remains undescribed.
One study classified Coloborhynchus among carnivorous pterosaurs, contrasting with other species classified as piscivores or insectivores.
Many analyses from 2019 and 2020 recovered Coloborhynchus within the family Anhangueridae, specifically in the subfamily Coloborhynchinae, which is the parent group of Coloborhynchus.

Coloborhynchus fossils have been found in the Lower Cretaceous of England, dating from 140 to 136 million years ago, and it was a pterodactyloid pterosaur of the family Ornithocheiridae that lived in Europe during the Early Cretaceous (Valanginian), approximately 135 million years ago.

Reginald Walter Hooley argued that the defining jaw trait was an artifact of erosion and that Coloborhynchus was indistinguishable from Criorhynchus simus, a view concluded by Hooley in 1913 and agreed with by Kuhn in 1967.
Rodrigues and Kellner disagreed with this classification, noting that both lacked the straight crest starting at the snout tip or teeth pointing to the sides as seen in C. clavirostris.
A 2023 review suggested that the traits distinguishing Nicorhynchus from Coloborhynchus were subtle enough to justify synonymizing the two genera.

Kellner, who considered Uktenadactylus a distinct genus in 2008, also considered Siroccopteryx different, noting it lacked the unique dental row characteristics of Coloborhynchus, a view supported by Fastnacht in 2001, and noted that C. sedgwickii lacks the unique characteristics of C. clavirostris and may even belong to the same genus as "Ornithocheirus" compressirostris, while C. capito is too incomplete for a full comparison with C. clavirostris, and its precise classification remains open to debate.
